analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent a tax rule that lets multinational companies defer US tax on certain foreign income.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in November 2019 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently extend a tax provision that lets US multinational companies avoid immediate US tax on certain income — dividends, interest, rents, and royalties — that flows between their foreign subsidiaries, including ones set up in low-tax jurisdictions. Without the rule, that income could be taxed under anti-deferral rules targeting passive foreign income. The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: US multinational corporations with foreign subsidiaries would gain if the bill passed, by keeping a permanent exemption from subpart F anti-deferral tax rules for certain related-party foreign income. That income would continue to defer US tax indefinitely rather than being taxed as current passive income. Tax professionals advising these companies would also benefit from the certainty of a permanent rule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US multinational corporations and their shareholders

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the look-thru rule exempting related-party foreign income (dividends, interest, rents, royalties) from subpart F anti-deferral taxation.
Allows indefinite deferral of US tax on that income, rather than treating it as current taxable passive income.
Would apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2019.

analysis.who_pays: US taxpayers generally would bear the cost of the forgone revenue, since permanent deferral of corporate foreign income reduces federal receipts that must otherwise come from other tax sources or borrowing.
analysis.who_pays_short: US taxpayers through forgone federal revenue

drawbacks.text: Permanently exempts income that can be routed through low-tax jurisdictions from anti-deferral rules designed to catch passive foreign earnings.
Reduces federal revenue permanently, shifting the tax burden to other taxpayers or adding to deficits.
The rule is a carve-out from subpart F, a law meant to prevent US companies from shifting profits to tax havens.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a permanent, targeted tax benefit to multinational corporations at the cost of federal revenue and reduced anti-avoidance enforcement. There is little in the bill for ordinary working people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. Ron Kind (D-WI) on November 21, 2019 with 14 cosponsors (8 Republicans, 6 Democrats).
Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction; no further action recorded.
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US taxpayers kept the existing status quo rather than gaining a permanent corporate carve-out from subpart F anti-deferral rules. No one gained from the bill itself; multinational corporations simply did not receive the permanent deferral benefit they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: US taxpayers, by avoiding a permanent corporate tax carve-out

for.name: Rep. Ron Kind
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the look-thru rule permanent.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Democrat and its cosponsors split evenly between 8 Republicans and 6 Democrats; no one opposed it, but the Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Would gain indefinite deferral of US tax on certain foreign income now caught by anti-deferral rules, reducing their US tax bill.
A permanent rule provides certainty and planning value for advisers serving multinational clients.
